articles.text: Nothing signals the start of summer in Piedmont quite like the sight of Cub Scouts taking over Dracena Park. The annual, week-long Cub Scout Day Camp kicked off on Monday, June 12, and will run through late Friday afternoon when the celebrated Egg Drop signals the conclusion of summer camp at Dracena Park. Piedmont Scout Council Executive Director Kate Benson said that this year’s camp, with the theme “Off to the Races!”, is nearly full, with over 38 registered campers, more than double last year’s number. Although many campers are current Cub Scouts, the day camp is open to all youth, whether Scouts or not. Camper Ronan Earle shows off his Cub Scout “Racing License.”

articles.text: Hillsides to be cleared by goats starting next week Piedmont has retained the services of approximately 200 goats for its annual summer cleanup of the hillsides surrounding the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. The goats, which reduce fire hazards by eating dry vegetation on city property, are a popular sight each year at the beginning of summer. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan said that although the date of their arrival has not been set, the goats ­ – coming from Ecosystem Concepts Inc. – are expected to arrive in Piedmont sometime next week after they complete their current shrub-eating job at Oak Knoll, near the Oakland Zoo. The four-legged grazers will begin their work on the large slope behind the Corporation Yard, and will later be moved across Moraga Avenue to Blair Park. Their vegetation-eating is crucial in light of the impending fire season, as it is a natural way to prevent ladder fuel from forming. Brannigan has said that a good rule of thumb to prevent ladder fuel — a firefighting term for vegetation which carries a fire from the landscape upward to tree or shrub canopies — is to leave three times the amount of space above. articles.text: Editor: As this school year ends, we are feeling hopeful again for the future of PUSD in ways we couldn’t have imagined a few years ago. A big part of that hopefulness is due to the leadership of our interim superintendent, Donald Evans, over the last year. From the start, Dr. Evans approached his new job with curiosity and openness – rather than the defensiveness and lack of transparency we had grown used to. He showed an eagerness to engage with and listen to *all* stakeholders in the district, rather than sowing division, which only undermines kids’ educations. He brought a positive energy and lightness to School Board meetings that had been missing. Instead of offering a set of excuses to justify inertia and status quo, he responded to challenges and problems with a solution-oriented mindset. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department has announced the beginning of its “Cop on the Block” program, a yearlong series of community outreach events. Though many of the men were veterans of various branches of the military, there was a belief that slavish obedience to commands was counterproductive, so the Balloon Platoon was born. articles.text: For the 20th year, the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band will take a lead position in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade, with its parasol-toting, shuffle-stepping Grand Marshal leading the way. Zenith, a Berkeley-based group, lays claim to being the most authentic brass band playing the music of old New Orleans from the formative years of 100 years ago to the present. Parade bands in New Orleans are still part of the musical tradition in the Crescent City, playing for funerals, parades, picnics and dances. All members of the Zenith band have been playing in similar jazz bands in the Bay Area for many years. Its Grand Marshal leads the way, proudly holding a fringed parasol, wearing a colorful sash, and doing a shuffle step down the length of Highland Avenue. People dancing behind the band, sometimes swirling parasols, are known as the second line. Everyone is invited to join the second line. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band has been a major attraction for many years at Photo by Raymond Holbert Alan Carr has assumed the role of Grand Marshal of the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band for his late father, Hollis Carr. the New Orleans By the Bay production at Shoreline Amphitheater. It has been part of the Traditional Jazz portion of the Concord Jazz Festival for 17 years, and for the past seven years it has appeared at the Bodega Bay Fisherman’s Festival. The band plays each year at the Sacramento Jazz Jubilee in Old Town during June.

articles.text: On the last moment of the 2023 school year, Friday, June 2, at 11:59 a.m. and 50 seconds, Principal Carol Cramer started a 10 second countdown with Wildwood School 5th graders. The annual countdown for elementary school students, known as “the ruckus,” took on an additional meaning this year as it signaled the final seconds of Cramer’s career. At zero, students shouted and banged hand-held noise makers, while the flash of parents’ cameras captured the moment. Cramer’s career, which started in the classroom in 1984, culminated as the clock struck noon. Her 35 years in Piedmont School district began at Beach School in 1988, one block from her home, as a 2nd grade teacher. It ended on the lunch patio in the front of Wildwood School where 5th graders were cheerfully celebrating their advancement to middle school. Carol quietly picked up a bell given to her in her first year as Principal in 2000. The bell, now 5th grade teacher Lydia Tang (left), Principal Carol Cramer, Counselor Colleen Stormer, and 5th grade teacher Hannah Swernoff Carol Cramer counts down the final seconds of her career with Wildwood 5th graders on June 2, 2023. Principal Carol Cramer with Wildwood 5th graders on the last day of school, June 2 broken, sat on her desk for 23 years. For Cramer, the silence of the bell was welcome, as will be the absence of the bells designating lunch, recess and dismissal every day on the Wildwood campus. Cramer retires to a quieter life in her Piedmont home, with husband Jim and son Jack who will be entering his senior year at the high school.

articles.text: Common Sense, a national nonprofit organization dedicated to helping kids and families thrive in a world of media and technology, has recognized Piedmont Middle School (PMS) as a Common Sense School. The recognition acknowledges the school’s commitment to creating a culture of “digital citizenship.” Common Sense began making entertainment and technology recommendations for families and schools in 2003. Being named a common sense school acknowledges the schools commitment to taking a whole-community approach to preparing its students to think critically and use technology responsibly to learn, create, and participate while preparing them for the perils that exist in the online realm, such as plagiarism, loss of privacy, and cyberbullying. “We’re honored to be recognized as a Common Sense School,” said Principal Karyn Shipp. “By preparing our students to use technology safely and responsibly, we are providing them an opportunity to build lifelong habits to help them succeed in a tech-driven world,” she added. “Piedmont Middle School deserves high praise for giving its students the foundational skills they need to compete and succeed in the 21st-century workplace and participate ethically in society at large,” said Kelly Mendoza, vice president of education programs at Common Sense Education. To learn more about the criteria Piedmont Middle School met to become recognized as a Common Sense School and the organization’s efforts, visit Commonsense.org/education/recognition-schools.

articles.text: I think it’s time we face the truth. Curiosity did not, in fact, kill the cat. Actually, studies will say that staying curious for as long as possible can actually have positive effects on your long-term health and well-being. If you want to cultivate a creative mind, your first job is to cultivate a curious mind. A curious mind is looking at the world through a lens of “not knowing.” There is always the opportunity to have a beginner’s mindset with something new to learn around every corner. And that experience of discovery and seeing possibilities is an opportunity for creativity. A creative act brings something new into the world, but if you aren’t curious, you will never ask yourself, “What wants to be discovered here?” Even if you have done the same task over and over again, what is different about this particular moment in time? The Broadway actor does the same show over and over again, eight times per week, sometimes for years, but the performance has to feel new and fresh for every audience or the magic just won’t be there. How do those actors keep it fresh? They cultivate presence, moment to moment, noticing what How can we cultivate creativity in our daily routines? is unique and special about this particular show. They listen with intensity to their fellow actors, hearing the words from their mouths as if it is the first time they have ever heard them. They find ways to make things novel and fun. And, above all, they are curious, ready to see what the moment will deliver and open to receiving it. In essence, they continue to find opportunities for creativity, even within repetition. In our daily lives, we have so many tasks we perform by rote. What if we chose to bring our curious mind to cultivate the creative experience in the most mundane of tasks. What if today, we get curious about washing dishes? • • What sounds do I hear? What does the water feel like on my hands? • Does the viscosity of the soap remind me of anything? • How could I do this faster? What happens if I go slower? All of a sudden, something totally boring might become more interesting. And, you never know, maybe you will invent something that will revolutionize dish washing and we will never have to do it again. More time to spend with the cat! articles.text: Piedmont resident Guy Avagliano did what many have dreamed of doing. In the span of 59 days, he took an all-American trip this spring, visiting all 30 Major League baseball stadiums. Avagliano took the long way. Leaving Oakland on April 2, he arrived in San Francisco at Oracle Park 16,000 miles later on May 30. After retiring as an actuary at the start of the year, Avagliano realized he might have time to tackle the two-month trip. “I’ve always been a baseball fan, but the appeal to me was to do this in one long road trip,” said Avagliano. “It kind of started out as a fun math puzzle from a logistical standpoint, to be able to get to all those stadiums on days when there were games.” Guy Avagliano (left) at Chase Field in Phoenix, Arizona on April 9 with childhood friend Greg McIntyre. Along the way Avagliano visited seven new state, incresing his tally to a complete 50 by taking detours to reach Arkansas and Maine. He also visited six baseball museums and 15 minor league baseball stadiums. Avagliano said the mystique and antiquity of Wrigley Field made it his favorite stadium. The St. Louis Cardinals had the best crowd, while Atlanta had the nicest new stadium. A beignet in New Orleans was the best food he ate, and the Tampa Bay Rays are his pick to win the World Series later this fall. The adventures before each first pitch and after the ninth inning gave the trip true meaning. After a Facebook post announcing his intention to take the trip, he got a call from a longlost childhood friend, Greg McIntyre, inviting him to stay in Arizona when he visited the stadium in Phoenix. Guy’s wife, Alison, confirmed the pair had not seen each other in 50 years. “Yeah, well he was pretty cool when he was 10,” noted Guy. Avagliano took the family SUV, a 2013 Infiniti with 180,000 miles on it. He had three unexpected auto repairs, including one near the Arizona–New Mexico border, but none of them caused a change of plans. Avagliano, who has lived in Piedmont since 2000, is originally from Maplewood, NJ so he scheduled some extra days on the East Coast part of the trip. In addition to seeing his only living aunt and uncle in New Jersey, he also saw 13 first cousin and five second cousins. “I saw my grandparents’ houses, my kindergarten, my first little league field, my first church. That was that just the best day, and there wasn’t even any baseball that day,” he said. Guy credits Alison, who joined him for part of the trip, for her support in making it a successful journey. “Alison was a real trooper throughout this. We even spent our 25th anniversary on the road, We had brunch in her hometown, Asheville, NC, then spent 500 miles driving to my cousin’s house to stay with people she’s never met,” he said. Sometimes the best parts of a journey happen when you least expect it. After leaving a minor league game in the ninth inning, a foul ball left the stadium and bounced a few feet away for him to pick up. Foul balls, road trips and life, are sometimes all about being in the right place at the right time. Upon returning home on May 30 from his epic tour of Major League ballparks, the big screen in Oracle Park in San Francisco honors the completion of Guy Avagliano’s journey. articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s boys’ and girls’ soccer teams celebrate winning the North Coast Section championship at the same time – at Beach Chalet Soccer Field in San Francisco on February 25. The 2022-23 school year has officially concluded at Piedmont High with teams turning the page on another sports calendar. In this article, the Post reflects on our favorite five moments from the past year. 1. February 25 an historic day Saturday, February 25 marked an historic day for Piedmont High. The boys’ soccer team, girls’ soccer team, and girls’ basketball team won the North Coast Section championship – and all on the same day. All four of Piedmont’s winter sports teams reached the NCS semifinals – a feat rarely accomplished. The boys’ soccer team, the No. 8 seed, started the legendary day with a 1-0 upset victory over No. 2 University, winning backto-back Div. 4 NCS championships. William Daniel scored the game-winner with 10 minutes left in regulation. The Highlanders did not allow any goals in the postseason, winning 2-0 over No. 9 St. Helena in the first round, devastating No. 1 Cardinal Newman 1-0 in the quarterfinals, beat No. 5 Healdsburg 1-0 in the semifinals, and then upending the University Red Devils at Beach Chalet Field in Golden Gate Park. articles.text: Hurricane Diane, presented by Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre, will premiere this Friday, June 16. Written by Madeleine George, the play follows protagonist Carol, a seemingly ordinary if not materialistic woman. who resides on a cul-de-sac in New Jersey. One day, she is visited by the Greek god Dionysus, under the guise of a lesbian gardener named Diane. Diane is determined to reverse climate change and restore earthly order by seducing a band of mortal followers. She sets out to woo Carol from her picture-perfect suburban life. George, a Pulitzer Prize finalist, calls it a “hilarious evisceration of the blind eye we all turn to climate change and the bacchanalian catharsis that awaits us, even in our own backyards.” Hurricane Diane is directed by Jennifer King. Post show discussions will be held on June 23, June 27, July 5 and July 13. Purchase tickets at www. auroratheatre.org, at by calling the box office at (510) 843 - 4822.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s (ACT) production of the beloved classic Wizard of Oz is playing onstage in San Francisco now through June 25. The classic tale by L. articles.text: Among the cornucopia of flowers which the de Young Museum’s annual Bouquets de Art brought to San Francisco last week, the floral design by Valerie Lee’s team bloomed for the gazing crowds. The annual event ended on Sunday, June 11, marking its 39th year of being the most widely-attended event at the museum. Veteran designers exhibiting at the show are allowed to choose their favorite art pieces in the museum’s collection and then are given their muse, based on a lottery, to emulate with a flower design. Now in her 24th consecutive year as an exhibitor, Lee chose Alexander Pope’s “The Wild Swan” painting from 1900 for its “stark drama and contrast of dark and light,” as well as for the painting’s vivid gold frame. “I love the idea of inviting the community at large to view and enjoy flowers, creativity and art at the de Young Museum,” said Lee. “There is such a local following with this show, which makes it very exciting and engaging for me. Many of our J. Miller customers, friends from Piedmont, and Piedmont Garden Club friends look forward to this annual show.” Over 100 floral designers hailing from throughout the Bay Area participated in Bouquets to Art this year. “I especially love how all ages and generations can enjoy The floral display by J. Miller Flowers at the annual Bouquets to Art exhibit at the deYoung Museum in San Francisco is a tribute to Alexander Pope’s 1900 painting, “The Wild Swan”. the f lower-filled galleries,” Lee added. “My children have attended the show for 24 years, and now they bring their friends, attend the gala, and even assist with my exhibit.” For her display, she chose to use phalaenopsis orchids, peonies, calla lilies, parrot tulips, lilacs, smokebush and succulents – a unique yet faithful textural interpretation of the stark whites and subtly shaded greens and yellows in Pope’s painting. articles.text: Visit the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art to view its newest exhibition, Frank Bowling: The New York Years 1966–1975, the first major exhibit of the artist’s work in North America in 40 years. Sir Richard Sheridan Patrick Michael Aloysius Franklin Bowling, known as Frank Bowling, was born in British Guiana, now Guyana, and moved from London to New York. He is best known for his large-scale, abstract and colorful paintings, color field painting and lyrical abstraction; sometimes referred to as ‘abstract expressionism.’ SF MOMA’s exhibition features 45 vibrant and largescale paintings, and a selection of archival materials such as recorded interviews of the artist in New York and London, film footage and photographs from Bowling’s 1968 visit to Guyana. “We are looking forward to engaging our communities with the exceptional work of Frank Bowling and to offering an in-depth exploration of the enduring influence of his time in New York, both on his own work and on the development of art more broadly,” said Christopher Bedford, the Helen and Charles Schwab Director at SFMOMA. “In particular, the presentation of the 5+1 exhibition provides an opportunity to experience Bowling as a scholar and teacher committed to elevating the voices of Black artists and expanding the understanding of art history as it unfolded. This very much aligns with our institutional vision to share significant, if perhaps lesser-known, facets of artists’ careers and to explore artistic achievement through a spectrum of lenses and perspectives.” The New York Years opened May 20, and will be on display through September 10. The exhibition is co-organized with the Museum of Fine Arts Boston. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit www.sfmoma.org. Frank Bowling, Elder Sun Benjamin, 2018

articles.text: Martin Scorsese, director extraordinaire, once commented that before becoming enamored with filmmaking he considered the priesthood. Filmgoers and critics have noted that the brittle tension between faith and the human condition haunts many of his films. Silence, made in 2016, may be his most overt and obscure film to date, one in which he examines the extraordinary lengths men and women have been willing to go to sustain their beliefs, even when confronted with what can only be characterized as profound silence. The film is set in Japan. The year is 1640. It was a time when Catholic priests journeyed throughout Europe and Asia, proselytizing their faith, searching with more than a hint of fanaticism for converts. Silence opens with Father Cristovao Ferreira, sinking to his knees, his face a mask of pain and agony, as he watches several crucified priests splashed with boiling water from a hot spring, by Japanese soldiers, to the point of being scalded to death. The film then cuts to two young Jesuit priests seated before their superior, Father Valignano (Claran Hinds), who reads to them a letter from Father Ferreira in which he admits that he has forsaken his religion and now lives as a Japanese resdent. The two Portuguese priests, Father Sebastio Rodriques (Andrew Garfield) and Father Francisco Garupe (Adam Driver), listen in disbelief. They were mentored by Father Ferreira (Liam Neeson) and refuse to believe that he would apostatize. They plead with Father Valignano to permit them to travel to Japan in the hopes of finding their teacher. Liam Neeson stars in Silence Father Valignano understands the danger that Japan represents – it was a country that resisted most harshly the presence of what it considered arrogant European priests who would attempt to convert the people, At first he says no. But hearing the pleas of the two priests he finally relents, reminding them that they will be the last priests ever go to Japan. And so the journey of the two profoundly naïve, yet deeply religious young priests begins. It was a pilgrimage they never could have imagined, filled with unintended consequences. At first protected by a small Christian cult, they hide in caves and a shack, fearful that they will be discovered, always asking if anyone has heard of Father Ferreira. No one has. They also fear being discovered by a man known as The Inquisitor (Issei Ogata) whose mission it is to extirpate this incompatible religion and its adherents from his country. He gives each convert the opportunity to step on what is called the fumi-e, a small plaque bearing a resemblance of Christ or Mary. If they refuse they are tortured: drowned, beheaded or crucified. Father Rodrigues is ultimately captured and forced to bear witness to the horror the Japanese Christians must endure. It is almost more than he can bear and at one point he says, “I pray but I am lost. Am I praying to silence?” This is a dark and painful film to watch. But it is also profound in its construction. Some in the audience may feel it’s a long, difficult slog, for what Father Rodrigues is compelled to watch is oft repeated. He knows he can put a stop to the torment, his own and the Japanese Christians, if he will only yield his faith and become an apostate. What is remarkable throughout the film is the presence of the question that Father Rodrigues asks: “Am I praying to silence?” It is a fundamental interrogatory, embedded in all religion. Those early films (The Big Sleep, D.O.A.) were moody, stylized, shot in black and white and derivative of the period’s gritty, hardboiled crime novels, also known as pulp fiction. A contemporary example is Drive. At first blush this film may seem like just another car chase film, similar to the Transporter franchise. Drive, however, is far more than gleaming muscle cars racing along the dark streets of L.A. with the cops or bad guys in hot pursuit. Rather, it is in the best tradition of the noir genre and pulp cinema. It is economical in plot and dialogue, with a central character – a man with no name, called simply Driver (Ryan Gosling), He is laconic to a fault, possessing no history other than now. He is a Hollywood stunt driver who moonlights as a getaway driver for robbers, and as a mechanic for an old friend, Shannon (Bryan Cranston), who owns a garage in a frayed part of town. As a character, Driver follows Eastwood and McQueen, two consummate actors who turned detachment and isolation into an art form. It was a time when Catholic priests journeyed throughout Europe and Asia, proselytizing their faith, searching with more than a hint of fanaticism for converts. Silence opens with Father Cristovao Ferreira, sinking to his knees, his face a mask of pain and agony, as he watches several crucified priests splashed with boiling water from a hot spring, by Japanese soldiers, to the point of being scalded to death. The film then cuts to two young Jesuit priests seated before their superior, Father Valignano (Claran Hinds), who reads to them a letter from Father Ferreira in which he admits that he has forsaken his religion and now lives as a Japanese resdent. The two Portuguese priests, Father Sebastio Rodriques (Andrew Garfield) and Father Francisco Garupe (Adam Driver), listen in disbelief. They were mentored by Father Ferreira (Liam Neeson) and refuse to believe that he would apostatize. They plead with Father Valignano to permit them to travel to Japan in the hopes of finding their teacher. Liam Neeson stars in Silence Father Valignano understands the danger that Japan represents – it was a country that resisted most harshly the presence of what it considered arrogant European priests who would attempt to convert the people, At first he says no. He gives each convert the opportunity to step on what is called the fumi-e, a small plaque bearing a resemblance of Christ or Mary. If they refuse they are tortured: drowned, beheaded or crucified. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honore’ The Transformers film franchise made its debut in 2007, followed by four sequels, each directed by Michael Bay and each, incrementally, shredding the original charm and solid story telling. Bay seemed content to indulge his predilection for CGI chaos, over-the-top histrionics, explosions, and bot slams. In every way the recently released Bumblebee (a prequel) is not only redemptive, but resurrects that sweet spot mined by Shia LaBeof, as Sam Witwicky, in the first Transformers when he negotiates with his dad for a car. He finds a hard-used, yellow Camaro on a lot and convinces his dad that this rusty ride works for him. And so his adventure begins. Ditto Charlie Watson (Hailee Steinfeld), who is on the cusp of turning 18 and declares that, like Sam, all she wants is a car. Any After a brief lead-in segment where the Autobots/Optimus Prime and the Decepticons/Megatron are locked in a destructive battle on Cybertron, their home planet, the narrative shifts to 1987. The place is the San Francisco Bay Area. Charlie is grieving for her father who died two years before of a heart attack while they were restoring a vintage Corvette that still sits in the garage. As it turns out, she’s an appealing but rebellious gear head who works on old cars at a local garage when she’s not going to school. She also feels unheard and alienated at home. Her mom (Pamela Adion) has remarried, her stepdad is okay, and her younger brother is doing just fine. It’s Charlie who feels adrift. Nosing around the junk-laden garage where she hangs out daily, Charlie discovers a vintage yellow VW Beetle hidden under a tarp. She is immediately smitten and pleadingly negotiates with the owner of the garage for this clearly abandoned ride. As it turns out, the key is in the ignition, the engine works and, with the owners blessing (Happy Birthday, he tells her), she’s soon driving off toward home and that empty spot next to her dad’s Corvette. With the Beetle safely in the garage, she walks around its exterior and decides to check its undercarriage. It’s at his moment that there is a classic and wondrous reveal. As she is shinning a light under the rusty chassis, she sees two large aqua blue eyes looking back at her. Abruptly, unexpectedly, the benign-looking VW transforms and there standing before her is a huge banana yellow bot. It’s a meet cute scene that ends with a startled, at-first-disbelieving Charlie naming the Transformer Bumblebee. As she learns, he proves to be a gentle, even timid, giant. And after catching her breath, she and B.B. tentatively bond. Actually, as it turns out, both, in a way, are hiding out – though for B.B. the stakes are much higher. They begin what proves to be a touching friendship. It’s at this point in the story that Charlie’s adventure begins. This is a relationship story. Even when the Decepticons locate Bumblebee (who we learn from the initial set up that he is on a mission for Optimus Prime), the film doesn’t drop off a cliff into vacuous violence that became the brand for the five sequels. Bumblebee is a genuinely good movie that engages and entertains. It’s perfect for those tweens and newbie teens who likely don’t have a clue what life was like in 1987, but understand what it feels like to discover a bot in their home garage. The film comes along at Christmas time, and beckons to parents and kids alike to spend two hours with this Hasbro endorsed tale that has the iconic E.T. embedded in scene after scene. It is distinctly a user-friendly family film. Bumblebee. Directed by Travis Knight. Starring Hailee Steinfeld, John Cena and Pamela Adion. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Part 63 in a biweekly series What impressed me most during a recent trip to Portugal was the incredible Urban Design found there! As many readers of this column know by now, this field of environmental design is my favorite and something I feel very strongly about. Urban Design can at its core be defined as the responsive siting of buildings and the design of the spaces between them. It involves the coordination of the associated design fields of Planning, Architecture, and Landscape Architecture all working together to produce (hopefully) interesting, active, community enhancing public and civic spaces. This concept is vitally important in our built environment and yet has been little understood and often neglected during much of the last century, a time when our focus has been, often exclusively, on individual buildings. A way for us to re-learn this area of critical design is to look around and study examples in other parts of the state, country and world. At the largest size, the Avenida de Liberdade in Lisbon, is a wonderful tree-lined grand boulevard and view corridor connecting the newer city on high ground to the Tejo River below. It is a linear park filled with every manner of monument, shop and seating place. At a much smaller scale, the Proaca Luis square, also in Lisbon, is one of many such community gathering places, with adjacent bus stops, taxi stands, historical monuments, food kiosks, and places for street musicians. Walkers cover Grand Avenue By Dick Carter The Walking on Wednesdays group hadn’t walked the length of Grand Avenue in Piedmont in over a year, so they planned to walk it on June 7. There was a strong, first week of summer vacation turnout of 42 walkers and two K-9 best friend on hand at the Exedra. The walkers headed off down Magnolia Avenue past the quiet high school, and the not so quiet construction site for the CommuGrand Ave Church Oakland from the Tribune, Sun, Mar 22, 1953. Piedmont - 12 train - Grand Avenue. Piedmont - Grand Ave 1908 Photo nity Pool. The group continue to San Carlos Avenue, which might also be called Rose Avenue for all the beautiful flowers in the front yards. They crossed Oakland at Latham, the only road named Street in Piedmont. They went to a traffic island at the bottom of Lower Grand Avenue where they stopped for a group photo in front of the original entrance to the Piedmont Manor real estate neighborhood whose first home was sold in 1906. At Arroyo Avenue the history of Grand Avenue from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s past Post articles was shared. Back in the 1870s, today’s Grand Avenue was known as Pleasant Valley Road. It ran from Lake Merritt to the Piedmont hills. Today, the street in Piedmont is Grand Avenue until it crosses the Oakland city line where it becomes Pleasant Valley again. At what is now Grand and Linda Avenues a restaurant named “A Mon Chateau” (My Castle) was built in 1892. Over time it had a number of owners and a troubled history with the police because of owner and patron behaviors, which included having no liquor licenses and gambling. In 1914 the building became the Grand Avenue Grocery Company and the Del Monte Market in 1922. In 1929 the Piedmont City Council adopted an ordinance that allowed businesses from the city line to Linda Avenue on the west side of Grand Avenue, and to Fairview Avenue on the east side. Seven months later voters rejected another zoning ordinance to extend the business district to Oakland Avenue. Today, the business district on Grand Avenue remains the same as it was in 1929. In the 1930’s Piggly Wiggly, a division of Safeway, opened a second grocery store up the street at the corner of Sunnyside and Grand. The competition was stiff for the Del Monte Market. It floundered and closed, and the A Mon Chateau building was torn down. A series of gas stations later occupied the site. Finally, in 1987 the block-long, current Piedmont Financial Center was built. Further down the street was a not very successful “Big T” grocery store, which eventually became today’s Ace Hardware. At Linda Avenue the walkers noted the site of the former A Mon Chateau restaurant. They continued to Ace Hardware, then made the long, uphill walk back to the Exedra via Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues, completing a three-mile walk. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. A turnout of 42 walkers and two K-9 best friends participated in a walk on Grand Avenue on June 7. articles.text: When California winemakers started to get serious about making world class wine in the 1960s they looked to two regions of France for guidance. From Bordeaux they imported Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc and from Burgundy they imported Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. These two wine regions have been the dominant influences ever since. But in the last two decades another area of France has become a major influence on California wine production -- the Rhone Valley. About 30 years ago wine writer Robert Parker began touting the Rhone area as the up-and-coming alternative to overpriced Burgundies and Bordeaux. Parker’s influence was pervasive and today, Cote Roties, Hermitages, and Chateauneuf du Papes from the Rhone, are among the most sought after of France’s wines. In the last three decades the production of Rhone style wines in California has increased dramatically. A Rhone style wine is defined as one made from any of the following official Rhone grapes (or combinations thereof) Syrah, Mouvedre, Grenache, Cinsault, Carignane, and Petite Sirah for the red wines, and Viognier, Grenache Blanc Marsanne, and Roussanne for white. There are now hundreds of wineries making this style of wine from southern California up to Washington state. But the capital seems to be Paso Robles in central California, now home to America’s finest producer of Rhone wines – Tablas Creek. In 1989 The Perrin family, owners of the famous Chateauneuf du Pape winery Chateau Beaucastel, and Robert Haas, an American wine importer, bought property on a limestone ridge near Paso Robles with a desire to make Rhone style wines in America. They brought over grafts of the vines that made the great Beaucastel and began propagating them in a nursery near the winery. Today Tablas Creek is producing America’s finest Rhone style wines. The winery makes a large number of wines but many sell out quickly. For availability, see www.vineyardbrands. com or www.tablascreek.com. Tablas Creek is an interesting winery to visit and they welcome visitors with admirable hospitality. Always best to call ahead, it is about a four-hour drive from Piedmont. Much of the Tablas Creek range of wines is also available at Wine.com. The following wines were selected from their current releases and are worth searching out. • 2022 Patelin de Tablas Rose This light-colored Provencal-styled Rose is made from Grenache, Mourvedre, Counoise and Vermentino. It is utterly charming with a nose of fresh strawberries that jumps out of the glass. In the mouth it is fresh and lively with notes of cherries. The finish is smooth and clean and leaves you wanting another sip. Great as an aperitif or as a porch pounder on a hot afternoon. • 2022 Patelin de Tablas Blanc This wine is made from seven different grapes – the majority being Grenache Blanc and Viognier. The Viognier provides a lovely, perfumed nose of honeysuckle and apricots. On the palate it is round and soft with terrific acidity and good structure. The perfect wine to serve with fish or seafood. • 2021 Esprit Blanc de Tablas This is a step up in intensity from the Patelin Blanc. Made from Roussanne, Picpoul, Grenache Blanc Bourboulenc and Clairette Blanche the wine has loads of tropical fruit, pineapple, and floral notes in its medium-bodied, pure, crisp and lengthy personality. It has good weight in the mouth and voluptuous fruit. It has beautifully integrated acidity and will be versatile on the dinner table. articles.text: Piedmont Flix Fest flexes with musical The first sound movie – The first so-called “talkie” – was a musical. Called The Jazz Singer, and starring Al Jolson, it came out in 1927. By 1930 people were not only sound-move crazy, they were movie-musical crazy as well. In fact for 30 years, until the 1960s, musicals were a movie staple. Piedmont’s 2nd Thursdays Flix Fest paid homage to them last week with one of the best: MGM’s The Band Wagon. The movie was presented to the audience by Piedmont resident Bob Hall, a theater reviewer with the Piedmont Post for 24 years. Starting with 1939’s The Wizard of Oz, the MGM studio, with its big budgets and big stars, became the leading Hollywood producer of lush technicolor musicals – Meet Me in St. Louis, An American in Paris, Singin’ in the Rain. The latter is an affectionate satire of the movies, while The Band Wagon, which came out a year later in 1953, is an affectionate satire of Broadway, in both its pretensions and its frivolity. Written by Betty Comden and Adolf Greene, and directed by Vincente Minnelli (who was married to MGM star Judy Garland long enough to produce a famous daughter), The Band Wagon zeros in on once-successful movie song-and-dance-man, Tony Hunter, played by Fred Astaire. Hoping to revive his career, Tony heads to Broadway, where he gets entangled in a pretentious, doomed musical version of Faust. His luck isn’t all bad, though. He also gets entangled with Gabrielle Girard, played by the stunning Cyd Charisse, who had perhaps the most spectacular legs in all movie history. And he gets to reunite with old pals, Lily and Lester Marton, played amusingly by Nanette Fabray and Oscar Levant. The story heads in a positive direction when the Faust cast decides to drop its pompous project in favor of a bright, cheerful show. That leads to lively numbers, particularly one featuring three quarreling babies, and the movie’s most famous sequence, the “Girl Hunt” ballet, a spoof of Mickey Spillane. Astaire and Charisse have another fine moment swaying to “Dancing in the Dark” in Central Park. The movie concludes with a rousing “That’s Entertainment.” Next month’s 2nd Thursdays Flix Fest, on July 13, will screen Stanley Kubrick’s noir classic, The Killing. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the Flix Fest takes place in the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required and can be done at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. You’re welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

While there she was set up on a blind date with Jim Nybakken, who was serving in the Navy at the time. Over 53 years later they were still the best of friends and partners. She was always ready to volunteer for projects and for people who needed help. Largely in recognition and appreciation of those efforts she and Jim were named Sea Ranchers of the Year in 2020. articles.text: Karin Mai, a former resident of Piedmont for many years, passed away peacefully at her home in El Dorado Hills, CA on June 3, 2023 at the age of 83. She lived courageously with cancer for 13 years and spent the last month of her life surrounded by friends and family. Born in Sacramento, CA on October 14, 1939, she was raised primarily in Oakland by her adoptive parents, Amy Wickland and Lloyd Welty. After graduating from Oakland High School in January 1957, she attended Bethany College in Lindsborg, Kansas for two years and graduated from the University of California in San Francisco. In 1960 she married Donald Fredric Mai, who she met while at school in Kansas. Spending much of their lives in Piedmont, Karin and Don also lived in Claremont, They moved to El Dorado Hills in 2017. In addition to working for more than 40 years as a Dental Hygienist, Karin was an active volunteer for every school and activity her children attended (swim team, Camp Fire Girls, band and theater, to name a few). With a heart for social justice, Karin was very involved with her church communities of St. Paul Evangelical Lutheran in Oakland, Good Shepherd Lutheran in Claremont, Global Volunteers, serving wherever there was a need in places like Tanzania, Vietnam, India, China, Russia, Peru, Mexico, Canada and Australia. Karin will be remembered by many friends and family around the world for her big heart, her welcoming smile, her generosity and her unending acts of service. Memorials for Karin will be held at St. Stephen’s Lutheran Church in El Dorado Hills, CA on Tuesday, June 13 at 2:00 p.m. and at St. Paul Lutheran Church in Oakland on Saturday, August 19 at 1:30 p.m. Karin is survived by her husband, Don Mai, her children Jody (Devin) Bader, Stephen (Debbie) Mai and Darin (Kristin) Mai, and seven grandchildren, Amy (Nick) Bader, Jadin Bader, Jakin (Hannah) Mai, Jordan (Courtney) Mai, Kelsea Mai, Layla Mai and Olivia Mai, and four great grandchildren, Lydia Mai, Ainsley Mai, Piper Mai and Davie Mai. These thick woods are believed to breathe in toxins and breathe out fresh air, cleansing Paris. Bois de Boulogne is in a ritzier part of town than Bois de Vincennes east of the city. Just west of the Eiffel Tower, where the Seine bends southward, the Bois de Boulogne is wholly located in the 16th arrondissement. These woods were hunting grounds for the kings of France dating back a thousand years. A maze of bridle paths crisscross through the stands of tall trees. Only a few minutes’ drive into the more southerly woods opens to the Hippodrome racecourse. Refitted in 2018 with spectacular viewing stands and adding Paris-Longchamp to its Hippodrome name, its 82 acres are designated for steeplechase with an obstacle-course of fences and moats, with grandstands for 50,000 spectators. Emperor Napoleon III ceded the woodland from the crown to the city of Paris and was present with his wife Empress Eugénie for the first Hippodrome. The races attracted a huge public and were a favorite scene for impressionists Edgar Degas and Edouard Manet. Bois de Boulogne reimagined in 1850s It was the job of the Emperor’s Minister of Public Works, Baron Haussmann (Georges-Eugène Haussmann), to reconstruct the land grant with roads, paths, and walking trails in Bois de Boulogne. Haussmann built an artificial waterfall and grotto, stocked the park with deer, planted a half a million trees, and designed an underground waterway for manmade ponds and lakes complete with their own islands. The Baron built riding stables, cafes, bandstands, places for boat rentals. His work also included a bird aviary, plant conservatory, and a small zoo. Only 12 years later she was First Lady, enchanting the nation with her nuanced, acculturated French manners, while France was enthralled by her fluency. Enormous crowds cheered the popular 35th American president John F. Kennedy. High society flocked to the 16th, the largest of the 20 arrondissements, attracted to the woodsy, airy climate as ideal for their country homes. The city of Paris under Haussmann’s direction designed wide boulevards to bring the woodlands into reach. French 19th Century popular culture swooned over the swanky urban but still country utopia. It’s a part of Paris where renters can upgrade to more spacious living quarters with abundant space to play. The woods comprise more than half of the arrondissement’s land area. Next to the woods are handsome, understated but ornate residential apartment buildings with lots of greenery and statuary, groomed pathways, children’s attractions, and open space for pets. These residences are immediately recognizable as Haussmann buildings, and they efficiently house residents in comfort and close to nature. Today’s commute traffic loads up on these straight, broad multilane Haussmann boulevards. I see no vacant storefronts among the upscale shops and restaurants lining the streets, and sidewalk cafés are busy with patrons enjoying an outing post Covid-19 confinement. The Baron was celebrated as a national hero, although not without plenty of gripes about bulldozing old Paris. The 16th district with its pleasing visual symmetry, wide boulevards, and well-kept public areas seems to have sprung from a clean canvass, where 18th Century design leaped off the drawing table into a sparkling new district. Their season came to a close on May 24 in a 11-10 loss to No. 5 Justin-Siena in Napa. It was easily one of the most entertaining and nerve wracking games of all sports throughout the season. Piedmont trailed 6-1 following the bottom of the second inning, but PHS stormed ahead 7-6 in the top-fourth. Justin-Siena went up 11-7 following the bottom of the sixth, but the Highlanders began tacking on runs in the top-seventh, bringing it back to 11-10 with two outs and the bases loaded. However, Justin-Siena got out alive by forcing a groundout to end the game. In the semifinals, PHS made headlines with a major 5-2 upset of No. 1 Fortuna. Piedmont only trailed the game 1-0 after the bottom-fourth and went ahead 2-1 the following inning—never relinquishing the lead. Even the first-round was exhilarating with a 4-3 win over No. 9 Branson that lasted 12-innings and stretched over two days, May 17-18. Dimitri Papahadjopulos had three-RBI games against Fortuna and Branson. Photo by Mark Aikawa Piedmont’s baseball team celebrates after defeating Branson 4-3 in 12 innings. Corinn Richards, PHS Class of 2022, earned a role as a freshman at Smith College.
